note: Documents written to make the parser wrong. Everything above tests that the right answer is found; this set tests that a plausible wrong answer is not. A corpus of only well-formed documents scores 1.000 and measures nothing, which is the trap a self-authored golden set falls into — so these were written to fail, and the ones that stopped failing are the fixes worth having.

resumes.note: Section words used as ordinary English inside bullets. 'I have experience with Docker' is not an EXPERIENCE heading, and 'good communication skills' is not a SKILLS heading — both are full sentences, and the heading matcher must require a line that is mostly just the heading.
text: - I have experience with Docker and used it to containerise four services.
- Built a deployment tool; the interests of the ops team drove the design.
- My activities included on-call rotation and writing the runbook.

resumes.note: Names that contain a slash or a dot and must not be split. CI/CD is one thing, not two; Node.js is one thing, not a sentence boundary; .NET keeps its leading dot.

The heading and its list on one line - 'Skills: Python, SQL'. Common in one-page resumes. The heading is doing two jobs, so it is recognised only on an exact lexicon hit: a partial match would make 'Languages Known: Tamil, English' a skills section, and every 'Label: value' line a section boundary.

A skills line polluted with eligibility text. '7.5 CGPA' and '2+ years' are requirements, not skills, and filing them under skills puts a number the ontology can never resolve into the unmapped queue for ever.
text: Python, Django, 7.5 CGPA, 2+ years experience, B.Tech degree
